Is an object a star or a galaxy, is a galaxy spiral or elliptical, is a variable star a Cepheid or an RR Lyrae? These are classification problems, the other major category of supervised learning next to regression. Their importance grows with the size of the surveys. Surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, Gaia and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory catalog hundreds of millions to billions of objects. Astronomers cannot examine each object, and telescope time for follow-up observations is limited and expensive.

Classification algorithms help prioritize targets. We can select candidates for rare metal-poor stars from photometry before investing in high-resolution spectroscopy. Colors and variability help identify quasar candidates among millions of point sources. Light curves let us classify variable stars and transient events in time for follow-up of interesting phenomena.

A regression model can predict any real value, but a probabilistic classifier must output class probabilities, which lie between 0 and 1. A linear model might predict probabilities above 1 or below 0, which have no meaning, so we cannot simply apply linear regression. Logistic regression solves this problem by mapping the unconstrained linear prediction to a valid probability. Despite its name, it is a classification method.

In this chapter we develop logistic regression from a probabilistic view. We compare discriminative models, which learn to separate the classes directly, with generative models, which learn how each class generates its data. Maximum likelihood then defines the loss of logistic regression. We train the model with gradient descent and treat regularization and other practical issues of training. Logistic regression is the entry point to classification and leads to the more complex methods of later chapters.

7.1 Binary Classification Fundamentals

How do we represent categorical class labels mathematically? Regression labels are numbers, such as stellar mass in solar masses, luminosity in ergs per second or temperature in kelvin. Classes have no numerical value of their own. Galaxy morphologies (spiral, elliptical, irregular), stellar spectral types (O, B, A, F, G, K, M) and object types (star, galaxy, quasar) are examples.

For binary classification, where we sort objects into one of two classes, the standard approach encodes the classes as 0 and 1. Examples are star (0) versus galaxy (1), non-variable (0) versus variable star (1), and non-transient (0) versus transient event (1). By convention, class 0 is the “background” or “default” class, and class 1 is the “target” or “positive” class of interest. In a transient detection system, for instance, we assign 1 to the rare transient events, which we want to find among many non-transient sources.

The binary encoding has a useful symmetry. If we swap the labels, we recover equivalent predictions by taking 1 minus the original probability. A model that gives probability 0.8 to class 1 (transient) gives \(1 - 0.8 = 0.2\) to non-transient events, which are class 1 after the swap. Asking for the probability that an object is a transient or that it is not a transient gives mathematically equivalent problems.

With the labels encoded as 0 and 1, a classification algorithm predicts the probability \(P(C_1|\mathbf{x})\) that an object belongs to class 1. Here \(\mathbf{x}\) represents the features of the object, such as colors, morphology (point-source minus model magnitudes) or Gaia astrometry (proper motions and parallaxes). Since the probabilities of all classes sum to 1, \(P(C_0|\mathbf{x}) = 1 - P(C_1|\mathbf{x})\) in binary classification. We assign an object to the class with the higher probability. The decision boundary, the surface in feature space that separates the two classes, lies where \(P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) = P(C_0|\mathbf{x}) = 0.5\).

For a linear classifier, the decision boundary in a two-dimensional feature space is a line. A new object is classified by its side of this line, as Figure 7.1 shows.

7.2 Discriminative vs. Generative Models

How do we build a model of the probability \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x})\) that an object belongs to class \(k\)? There are two distinct paths, both connected through Bayes’ theorem \[ P(C_k|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}|C_k) \cdot P(C_k)}{p(\mathbf{x})}. \]

Discriminative Approach

The discriminative approach models \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x})\) directly, the posterior probability of class \(k\) given the features. This is the quantity that classification needs. It learns the boundary between the classes. For stars versus galaxies, the model takes the input features \(\mathbf{x}\), which may include dozens of measurements. It outputs the probability of each class, for example “this object has an 80% chance of being a galaxy.” It maps complex inputs to class probabilities without modeling how the features are distributed within each class.

Generative Approach

The generative approach takes the other path through Bayes’ theorem. Instead of modeling \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x})\) directly, it models the two components needed to compute it indirectly. The first is the distribution \(p(\mathbf{x}|C_k)\) of the features within each class, the class-conditional density, also called the likelihood. The second is the prior probability \(P(C_k)\) of each class. Bayes’ theorem then multiplies the two and normalizes by \(p(\mathbf{x})\) to give \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x})\).

The approach is called generative because it models enough about each class to generate new examples. For stars versus galaxies, it learns separately what stars look like, with their colors, point-like appearance and proper motions. It also learns what galaxies look like, with their extended shapes, color distributions and lack of proper motion. Figure 7.2 compares the two approaches for a single feature.

An analogy with language identification shows the difference. A discriminative approach to telling German from Portuguese would focus on features that differ. German might have more hard consonants and Portuguese more nasal sounds. It learns just enough to tell the two languages apart.

A generative approach would instead learn to speak both languages, with their grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation rules. This is much harder but teaches more. Someone who speaks both languages can distinguish them, generate new sentences and recognize dialects. Such a speaker also understands why certain sound combinations are valid in one language but not in the other.

A generative model can also detect outliers or new classes. A discriminative model has no density over \(\mathbf{x}\). Someone who only knows how to tell German from Portuguese (the discriminative model) might label Finnish as one of them with a probability close to 1. A fluent speaker of both languages (the generative model) would recognize that Finnish differs from both. In mathematical terms, both \(p(\mathbf{x}|\text{German})\) and \(p(\mathbf{x}|\text{Portuguese})\) are small.

A discriminative model trained only on stars and galaxies might label a quasar as one or the other with a probability close to 1. A generative model can flag an object whose features have a low density under both classes as something possibly new and interesting.

7.3 Logistic Regression and the Sigmoid Function

Logistic regression is a discriminative method that models \(P(C_1|\mathbf{x})\) directly. Given our experience with linear regression, a simple first attempt is to model this probability as a linear function of the features \[ P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}. \] Here \(\mathbf{w}\) is the vector of model parameters and \(\mathbf{x}\) is the vector of input features. A constant 1 appended to \(\mathbf{x}\) provides the bias term, the intercept \(w_0\) of Chapter 4.

However, a linear model produces unbounded outputs. The predicted value can be any real number, such as \(-2.7\) or \(5.3\), as Figure 7.3 shows. A probability must lie in \([0,1]\), so a prediction such as 1.2 or 1.5 has no probabilistic interpretation. In regression, a prediction of 10.2 for a true value of 10.0 is a small error. A probability of 1.2 for a positive example is meaningless, even though it is only 0.2 above 1.

The unbounded behavior also distorts the fit. Consider class 1 points far from the boundary, for which a linear model might predict values such as \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} = 2\). Least squares counts this correct prediction as an error of 1 against the target value of 1, as large as the error of predicting 0. Least squares therefore pulls the boundary toward such points, which can misplace it, as Figure 7.4 shows.

We need a function that maps the linear predictor \(z = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}\) into the range of probabilities while keeping the decision boundary linear. The sigmoid function does this \[ \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}. \]

This S-shaped curve maps any real number to the range \((0,1)\), so it can represent a probability. For very negative \(z\), \(\sigma(z)\) approaches 0, and for very positive \(z\), it approaches 1. At \(z = 0\), \(\sigma(z) = 0.5\), which marks the decision boundary. Points far from the boundary therefore receive probabilities near 0 or 1, and points close to it receive probabilities near 0.5. Figure 7.5 shows the curve and the probability contours that it creates in feature space.

The sigmoid function follows from probabilistic reasoning, through the odds of the two classes. For binary classification, the odds measure the relative belief in the classes \[ \text{odds} = \frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{P(C_0|\mathbf{x})} = \frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{1-P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}. \]

Probabilities lie between 0 and 1, but the odds range from 0 to infinity. The logarithm of the odds, called the log-odds or the “logit” transformation, extends the range to all real numbers \[ \text{logit}(P(C_1|\mathbf{x})) = \ln\left(\frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{1-P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}\right). \]A linear predictor can take any real value, and so can the logit. We therefore model the logit with our linear function \[ \text{logit}(P(C_1|\mathbf{x})) = \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}. \]

To find the probability, we reverse the logit transformation. Exponentiating both sides and solving for \(P(C_1|\mathbf{x})\) gives \[\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{1-P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}\right) &= \mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} \\ \frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{1-P(C_1|\mathbf{x})} &= e^{\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}} \\ P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) &= \frac{e^{\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}}}{1 + e^{\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}}} = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}). \end{aligned}\]The sigmoid function therefore emerges when we model the log-odds with a linear function. It is also called the logistic function, which gives logistic regression its name. The model is linear in the log-odds, and the sigmoid function maps the log-odds to probabilities. Figure 7.6 shows this transformation for a linear predictor and its sigmoid.

The linear decision boundary is preserved. The boundary lies where \(P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) = 0.5\), which means \(\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}) = 0.5\), and this happens exactly when \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x} = 0\). The boundary is therefore linear in feature space, as we wanted.

In astronomical terms, the linear predictor \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}\) is now the log-odds that an object belongs to one class rather than the other. For star-galaxy classification, a log-odds of 2 means that the odds of a galaxy against a star are \(e^2 \approx 7.4\) to 1.

7.4 From Discriminative to Generative

Bayes’ theorem connects the discriminative view of logistic regression to a generative view. In logistic regression we assumed that the log-odds are a linear function \(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}\) of the features. This creates a hyperplane decision boundary in feature space. A hyperplane is a flat surface with one dimension fewer than the space it lies in, such as a line in 2D or a plane in 3D. Points with \(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} > 0\) belong to class 1, and points with \(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} < 0\) belong to class 0. The vector \(\mathbf{w}\) is perpendicular to the boundary and sets its orientation.

Which assumptions about the feature distributions \(p(\mathbf{x}|C_k)\) give rise to such a linear boundary?

One answer is that the features of each class follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution, with the same covariance matrix for all classes. This condition is sufficient, and other distributions can also give a linear boundary, so logistic regression does not require Gaussian features.

The Gaussian density of class \(k\) is \[ p(\mathbf{x}|C_k) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2} \det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)\right). \] The dimension \(D\) is the number of features. Each class has its own mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\), and all classes share the covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\). Geometrically, each class is a “cloud” of points with the same shape and orientation, centered at different locations.

We now show that Gaussian distributions with equal covariance matrices make the log-odds linear in the features. Here we write the bias \(b\) explicitly instead of appending a constant 1 to \(\mathbf{x}\), because \(b\) is where the class priors enter. Bayes’ theorem gives \[ \ln\left(\frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{P(C_0|\mathbf{x})}\right) = \ln\left(\frac{p(\mathbf{x}|C_1)P(C_1)}{p(\mathbf{x}|C_0)P(C_0)}\right). \]

The denominator \(p(\mathbf{x})\) of Bayes’ theorem cancels in the ratio. We now substitute the Gaussian assumption for \(p(\mathbf{x}|C_k)\). The normalization constants cancel as well, because the covariance matrix is shared. This gives \[ \ln\left(\frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{P(C_0|\mathbf{x})}\right) = \ln\left(\frac{P(C_1)}{P(C_0)}\right) + \ln\left(\frac{\exp(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1))}{\exp(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0))}\right). \] The first term, \(\ln(P(C_1)/P(C_0))\), represents our prior belief about the relative frequencies of the classes. The second term compares how well the features \(\mathbf{x}\) match the Gaussian distribution of each class.

We simplify the second term. By the properties of logarithms, the logarithm of the ratio of Gaussians becomes a difference \[ -\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1) + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_0). \] We expand each quadratic form, starting with the first \[ (\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1) = \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1. \] The product \(\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\) is a scalar, so it equals its transpose \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x}\) because \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) is symmetric, and the same holds for the second form. Substituting both expansions into the difference gives \[ \begin{aligned} -\frac{1}{2}(&\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} - 2\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1) \\ &+ \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} - 2\boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0) .\end{aligned} \]

The terms with \(\mathbf{x}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x}\) cancel because they have opposite signs and the same covariance matrix. This cancellation eliminates the quadratic terms in \(\mathbf{x}\), which would otherwise prevent a linear boundary. What remains is \[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0. \] Factoring out \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x}\) gives \[ (\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{x} - \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0). \]Adding back the prior term gives the final form \[ \ln\left(\frac{P(C_1|\mathbf{x})}{P(C_0|\mathbf{x})}\right) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b, \] where the weight vector is \[ \mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0), \] and the bias is \[ b = \ln\left(\frac{P(C_1)}{P(C_0)}\right) - \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0). \]

Interpreting Weights and Bias

The weight vector \(\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0)\) depends on the class means and the shared covariance. We expect the boundary to lie between the two class centers, so \(\mathbf{w}\) needs a component along \((\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0)\). This raw direction is not enough, because we must also account for how the classes are spread in feature space.

This is the role of \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\). It gives less weight to directions along which the classes spread widely. Depending on the covariance and the mean difference, it can preserve the original direction or rotate it to account for the spread of the classes. Figure 7.7 shows this for three covariance matrices.

The bias term \(b\) has two components. The first, \(\ln(P(C_1)/P(C_0))\), is the prior term for class imbalance. In a field where galaxies outnumber stars ten to one, for instance, it equals \(\ln(10)\). This moves the decision boundary toward the stars, as Figure 7.8 shows. The second term, \(-(1/2)(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)\), sets the position of the boundary, which passes through the midpoint between the class means when the priors are equal. When \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) changes, \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(b\) change together, so the boundary still depends on both the covariance and the class means.

As in the derivation of the sigmoid above, inverting the log-odds \(z = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b\) gives \[ P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b)}}. \]The Gaussian model with equal covariances therefore gives logistic regression with a linear decision boundary. We reached the same model from the discriminative assumption of linear log-odds, so the two views agree. Figures 7.7 and 7.8 show how the covariance and the class priors shape the boundary.

7.5 Limitations of Logistic Regression

The link between the generative and discriminative views clarifies the inductive bias of logistic regression. This bias is the set of assumptions that shapes how the model learns and generalizes. The model assumes that the classes are best separated by a linear boundary in feature space. When the features of the classes approximately follow Gaussian distributions with similar covariance matrices, this assumption holds and logistic regression is a suitable classifier. In that case the linear boundary is the optimal one, because it assigns each object to the class with the higher posterior probability.

The success of a machine learning method depends on how well its inductive bias matches the structure of the data. The parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(b\) are tied to the class means, covariances and priors, so they encode the Gaussian inductive bias. Understanding the bias helps us predict when logistic regression succeeds and when it fails.

How realistic are the Gaussian assumptions? In astronomy, different classes often have different covariance structures. Spiral galaxies might show a larger variance in some color indices than elliptical galaxies because their star formation histories vary more. In star-galaxy separation, the spread of the features of galaxies, with their varied morphologies and redshifts, typically differs from the tighter distribution of stellar features. Unequal covariances leave quadratic terms in the log-odds, and a linear boundary can then perform poorly. Poor performance of a linear boundary can hint that the classes are not Gaussian with a shared covariance matrix.

Another limitation appears when a line cannot separate the classes in feature space. A linear boundary cannot follow a curved boundary between the classes, however much data we provide.

Feature Transformations

Logistic regression remains a useful tool, largely because we can transform the input features. As in linear regression, we are not limited to the raw features \(\mathbf{x}\). We can use transformed features \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) that better satisfy our assumptions.

Consider separating stars from galaxies with the flux and the half-light radius of an object. Both are positive and span orders of magnitude, so their logarithms often fit the Gaussian picture better than the raw values do. Similarly, classes that form arcs or rings in feature space can become linearly separable in polar coordinates, as Figure 7.9 shows. The figure reports the accuracy, which is the fraction of objects that the line classifies correctly.

Creating new features that separate the classes better is known as feature engineering, and it has been important in astronomical classification. Common transformations include logarithms of fluxes (magnitudes), color indices computed from fluxes, concentration indices from different aperture measurements, and morphological parameters. Each transformation encodes domain knowledge about which features separate the classes better. When we write \(\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) instead of \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}\), we encode this astronomical understanding in the model.

In photometric classification of quasars, for instance, a cut in the \((u-g)\) versus \((g-r)\) plane can help select quasars at certain redshifts. Their ultraviolet excess makes them bluer in \(u-g\) than stars of the same \(g-r\). The transformation from fluxes to colors creates a feature space where the classes are more separable.

Interpretability

Logistic regression is also easy to interpret. The linear form \(\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) shows how each feature contributes to the decision. When the features are standardized to zero mean and unit variance and weakly correlated, a larger absolute weight means that the feature matters more. In star-galaxy separation, for example, a larger absolute weight for the concentration index than for \(g-r\) suggests that the concentration matters more.

Because the decision boundary is linear, we can also visualize it. In a two-feature space we can draw the line that separates the classes. In higher dimensions we can project onto the features with the largest absolute weights. This lets us check whether the model uses physically sensible criteria. Suppose that we use the concentration index and the color to separate stars from galaxies. We can then check that the boundary lies where physics suggests, since stars are more point-like and follow the stellar locus in color.

When a linear boundary in some feature space separates the classes reasonably well, logistic regression gives good accuracy, interpretability and speed. When it does not, we must find better feature transformations or turn to more complex models. Knowing what a model assumes about the data guides these choices.

7.6 Maximum Likelihood and Cross-Entropy Loss

How do we find the best parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(b\)? For Gaussian classes with equal covariance, the generative derivation gave the closed forms \(\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0)\) and \(b = \ln(P(C_1)/P(C_0)) - (1/2)(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_0^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}_0)\).

This solution is limited in practice, because real astronomical data often do not follow Gaussian distributions with equal covariances. We can instead fit the linear boundary directly with a discriminative model. As in linear regression, we use maximum likelihood estimation to find the parameters that maximize the probability of the observed training data. This principle underlies many loss functions in machine learning.

Each of the \(N\) observations \((\mathbf{x}_i, t_i)\) consists of the features \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and a binary label \(t_i \in \{0,1\}\). As in linear regression, \(t\) denotes the observed target. The model predicts the probability of class 1 through the sigmoid function \[ P(C_1|\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}) = y_i = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i), \] where \(\mathbf{w}\) again includes the bias, as in linear regression. In our star-galaxy example, \(y_i\) is the probability that the \(i\)th object is a galaxy.

The likelihood is the probability of the labels of the data set under the model. We assume that the observations are independent, which is standard but can fail in astronomy, where spatial and temporal correlations are common. The likelihood is then the product \[ L(\mathbf{w}) = \prod_{i=1}^N P(t_i|\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}). \] For each observation, the factor in the product depends on its true class. If \(t_i = 1\) (the object is a galaxy), the factor is \(y_i\). If \(t_i = 0\) (the object is a star), the factor is \(1 - y_i\).

We combine the two cases into a single expression \[ L(\mathbf{w}) = \prod_{i=1}^N y_i^{t_i}(1-y_i)^{1-t_i}. \] The exponents \(t_i\) and \((1-t_i)\) select the right factor. For a galaxy (\(t_i = 1\)), the second factor becomes \((1-y_i)^0 = 1\), which leaves \(y_i\). For a star (\(t_i = 0\)), the first factor becomes \(y_i^0 = 1\), which leaves \((1-y_i)\).

This is the Bernoulli likelihood from the conjugate priors of Chapter 5, but now a linear model sets the probability through the sigmoid transformation.

As in linear regression, we work with the negative log-likelihood, which turns the product into a sum. We take the negative because most optimization algorithms minimize. The sum is easier to compute. It also avoids numerical underflow, where a product of many small probabilities is rounded to zero because it is too small to store. The problem becomes the minimization of a loss, which measures how poorly the weights fit the training data \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = -\ln L(\mathbf{w}) = -\sum_{i=1}^N [t_i \ln y_i + (1-t_i)\ln(1-y_i)]. \]

We usually divide by the number of samples \(N\), so that the loss does not grow with the size of the data set. From here on, \(E(\mathbf{w})\) denotes this average loss \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N [t_i \ln y_i + (1-t_i)\ln(1-y_i)]. \] Without this normalization, more data would inflate the loss and require us to retune the learning rate of the optimization algorithm (Section 7.7).

This expression is the cross-entropy loss, a name that comes from information theory. Entropy measures the average information, or “surprise”, of a probability distribution. Cross-entropy is the average surprise when we use the model probabilities \(y_i\) to describe the true labels \(t_i\). Each label \(t_i\) defines a distribution that puts probability 1 on the true class, and the model gives class 1 the probability \(y_i\). Section 8.6 develops this link to information theory.

To see why this is a suitable measure for classification, consider a single data point. For a galaxy (\(t_i = 1\)), a correct prediction \(y_i \approx 1\) gives \(\ln y_i \approx 0\) and thus little penalty. An incorrect prediction \(y_i \approx 0\) gives \(\ln y_i \to -\infty\) and thus a severe penalty. For a star (\(t_i = 0\)), a prediction \(y_i \approx 0\) gives a small loss, while \(y_i \approx 1\) is heavily penalized.

Unlike least squares on the linear predictor, cross-entropy gives a correct prediction with a probability close to 1 almost no loss. Distant points on the correct side therefore no longer dominate the fit. The penalty for a severe mistake grows without bound.

The full optimization problem is \[ \mathbf{w}^* = \text{argmin}_{\mathbf{w}} \left\{-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[t_i \ln \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i) + (1-t_i)\ln(1-\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i))\right]\right\}, \] where \(\text{argmin}_{\mathbf{w}}\) denotes the value of \(\mathbf{w}\) that minimizes the expression.

Unlike linear regression, this problem has no closed-form solution, which means no explicit formula for \(\mathbf{w}\) like the least-squares solution of Chapter 4. The nonlinearity of the sigmoid function prevents us from solving for \(\mathbf{w}\) analytically by setting the derivatives to zero. We therefore need numerical optimization, in particular gradient descent, to find the parameters iteratively. Many models of later chapters need numerical optimization as well. The cross-entropy loss is convex in \(\mathbf{w}\) (Section 4.4), which means that it has a single basin. A local minimum is a point lower than the points near it, and a convex loss has no local minimum besides the lowest point.

7.7 Gradient Descent for Logistic Regression

To find the weights \(\mathbf{w}\) that minimize the cross-entropy loss, we explore the loss surface iteratively. The loss \(E(\mathbf{w})\) defines a surface over the space of weight vectors. Each point is a choice of weights, and its height is the loss, which measures how poorly those weights describe the data. Our goal is the lowest point, where the weights describe the data best.

Imagine standing on this surface and trying to reach the valley. A simple strategy is to feel the steepness and direction of the slope and to step downhill by an amount proportional to the steepness. We repeat this until the ground is flat, which corresponds to the minimum for a convex loss.

This intuition translates into mathematics. The slope at a point \(\mathbf{w}\) is the gradient \(\nabla E(\mathbf{w})\), a vector that points in the direction of steepest ascent in weight space. We therefore move in the negative gradient direction. A parameter \(\eta\), the learning rate, controls the size of each step \[ \mathbf{w}^{(\tau+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(\tau)} - \eta \nabla E(\mathbf{w}), \]where \(\tau\) indexes the iteration.

Figure 7.10 shows the path of gradient descent on the loss surface. Starting from a high-loss region, each step follows the negative gradient toward the minimum.

Deriving the Gradient

To use gradient descent, we need the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the weights, which we compute step by step. We start with the nonlinearity in our model, the sigmoid function, whose derivative has a simple form \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}\sigma(z)}{\mathrm{d}z} = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)). \]We can derive this directly from \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\). The chain rule gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}\sigma(z)}{\mathrm{d}z} &= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}z}\left(\frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\right) \\ &= \frac{e^{-z}}{(1 + e^{-z})^2} \\ &= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \cdot \left(1 - \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\right) \\ &= \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)). \end{aligned}\]

When we compute \(z = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}\) and evaluate \(\sigma(z)\), the same value gives the derivative \(\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\) at no extra cost. With this derivative, we can find the gradient of the loss. To find \(\partial E/\partial w_j\), we apply the chain rule step by step.

We first consider how \(y_i\) depends on \(w_j\) \[ \frac{\partial y_i}{\partial w_j} = \frac{\partial}{\partial w_j}\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i)(1-\sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i))x_{ij} = y_i(1-y_i)x_{ij}, \]where \(x_{ij}\) is the \(j\)th feature of object \(i\).

The derivative of the loss with respect to \(w_j\) is \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_j} &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[t_i \frac{\partial}{\partial w_j}\ln y_i + (1-t_i)\frac{\partial}{\partial w_j}\ln(1-y_i)\right] \\ &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[t_i \frac{1}{y_i}\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial w_j} + (1-t_i)\frac{1}{1-y_i}\frac{\partial (1-y_i)}{\partial w_j}\right] \\ &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[t_i \frac{1}{y_i}\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial w_j} - (1-t_i)\frac{1}{1-y_i}\frac{\partial y_i}{\partial w_j}\right]. \end{aligned}\]Substituting the expression for \(\partial y_i/\partial w_j\) gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_j} &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[t_i \frac{1}{y_i} - (1-t_i)\frac{1}{1-y_i}\right]y_i(1-y_i)x_{ij} \\ &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[t_i(1-y_i) - (1-t_i)y_i\right]x_{ij} \\ &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - y_i)x_{ij}. \end{aligned}\]The gradient vector is therefore \[ \nabla E(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - y_i) \mathbf{x}_i = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - t_i) \mathbf{x}_i. \]

The gradient is driven by the prediction error \((y_i - t_i)\), scaled by the features \(\mathbf{x}_i\) that led to the prediction. When a prediction is close to its label (\(y_i \approx t_i\)), the sample contributes almost nothing, so weights that already give correct predictions need no adjustment. When the prediction is wrong, the contribution depends on the size of the error and on the strength of the features behind it. Figure 7.11 shows these contributions.

A wrong prediction with a high probability for the wrong class, such as \(y_i = 0.9\) for a star, gives a larger gradient than one with a lower probability, such as \(y_i = 0.6\). A large feature vector \(\mathbf{x}_i\) enlarges the gradient further. The model therefore prioritizes fixing its worst errors.

Computing the gradient needs only three operations. We compute the current predictions \(y_i = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i)\), calculate the prediction errors \((y_i - t_i)\) and scale the features by these errors.

Inserting this gradient into the update rule, we update the weights at iteration \(\tau\) according to \[ \mathbf{w}^{(\tau+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(\tau)} - \eta \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i^{(\tau)} - t_i) \mathbf{x}_i. \]

7.7.1 Stochastic Gradient Descent

The gradient is simple, but each update requires a sum over all \(N\) labeled training examples. The cost per iteration therefore grows in proportion to \(N\), written \(\mathcal{O}(N)\). This becomes expensive for large astronomical data sets, which range from millions of objects to billions of measurements.

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses the fact that we do not need the exact gradient. A small random subset of the data, called a mini-batch, approximates the gradient \[ \nabla E(\mathbf{w}) \approx \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^M (y_i - t_i)\mathbf{x}_i. \] Here \(M\) is the batch size, the number of samples in the mini-batch. It is typically 32 to 128, much smaller than \(N\). If the batch is a uniformly random subset of the training set, its gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient. This means that it is correct on average.

This is like surveying galaxy properties. Measuring all galaxies gives the most accurate statistics, but a random sample gives reasonably good estimates. We can take many such samples in the time needed to measure that population. Similarly, SGD takes many steps in roughly the right direction in the time that gradient descent needs for a few exact steps.

As the \(1/\sqrt{N}\) scaling of Chapter 3 shows, larger samples give estimates of lower variance. Mini-batch gradients are noisier than the full gradient, but they allow many more parameter updates for the same computing time. The frequent updates give rapid progress early in training, when the weights are far from optimal. Figure 7.12 compares a gradient descent path with several SGD paths from the same starting point.

Unlike deterministic gradient descent, SGD can also use its noise to escape poor local minima in the non-convex problems common in machine learning (Chapter 15). The loss of logistic regression has no such minima, so here the main gain of SGD is speed. The noise of mini-batch sampling also acts as a mild form of regularization. The noise in the gradient estimates controls the trade-off between exploitation (following the gradient) and exploration (random perturbations). Smaller batches give noisier estimates.

Using mini-batches, the update rule becomes \[ \mathbf{w}^{(\tau+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(\tau)} - \eta \cdot \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^M (y_i - t_i)\mathbf{x}_i. \]

7.8 Hyperparameters and Regularization

Learning Rate Considerations

Besides the mini-batch sampling, the size of each step matters, and the learning rate \(\eta\) controls it. Think of the learning rate as the size of a wheel rolling down the loss surface. On a bumpy surface, a large wheel (large \(\eta\)) rolls over small bumps and valleys, which can help it escape local minima. It may also bounce erratically down steep slopes and miss deeper valleys. A small wheel (small \(\eta\)) follows the terrain precisely and can dig deep for better minima, but it may get stuck in minor depressions. On the single basin of logistic regression, only the speed and the overshoot matter.

In astronomical terms, the choice resembles slewing a telescope with coarse or fine adjustments. A large \(\eta\) is like coarse slewing, which covers large distances quickly but may overshoot the target. A small \(\eta\) is like the fine adjustment knobs, which are precise but slow for large movements. Figure 7.13 shows SGD paths for a small and a large learning rate.

Choosing Hyperparameters

The learning rate \(\eta\) and the batch size \(M\) are hyperparameters, parameters that control the learning process and are not learned from the data. Unlike the weights \(\mathbf{w}\), which gradient descent optimizes, hyperparameters must be chosen before training begins. This choice is difficult because we usually do not know the shape of the loss surface in advance. It resembles choosing the wheel size for terrain that we cannot fully see.

For simple problems, a grid search tries each value of a fixed list and keeps the one with the lowest validation loss (Chapter 4). We typically search learning rates on a logarithmic scale, for example \(\{10^{-4}, 10^{-3}, 10^{-2}, 10^{-1}\}\), to cover a wide range of values with few trials. We might try batch sizes that are powers of 2, for example \(\{32, 64, 128, 256\}\). In more complex models trained on graphics processing units, powers of 2 are preferred because the memory and compute architecture is optimized for such sizes. For logistic regression the choice matters little, and a simple grid search often suffices, even though more advanced tuning methods exist.

Learning Rate Schedules

A fixed learning rate is a compromise between fast progress and a precise result. For more complex problems, we often start with larger steps to reach the right region of parameter space quickly. We then take smaller steps to improve the solution. A simple schedule that does this is the inverse time decay \[ \eta^{(\tau)} = \frac{\eta_0}{1 + \gamma \tau}. \] Here \(\eta_0\) is the initial learning rate, \(\gamma\) is the decay rate, and \(\tau\) is the number of the training step, a whole number. Figure 7.14(a) shows this schedule.

This schedule fits the wheel analogy. At first, \(\eta \approx \eta_0\), and we use a big wheel that rolls quickly across the terrain. As the iteration \(\tau\) increases, the denominator grows and \(\eta\) shrinks, so we switch to a smaller wheel that follows the terrain more precisely. A larger decay rate \(\gamma\) gives a quicker transition to refinement, and a smaller \(\gamma\) keeps the exploration going longer.

Cosine annealing is a second schedule. It is inspired by annealing in metallurgy, where slowly cooling a heated metal lets its atoms settle into an ordered structure with fewer defects. We lower the learning rate along a cosine curve from \(\eta_0\) toward a minimum value \(\eta_{\text{min}}\) over a cycle of \(T\) steps \[ \eta^{(\tau)} = \eta_{\text{min}} + \frac{1}{2}(\eta_0 - \eta_{\text{min}})\left(1 + \cos\left(\frac{\tau\pi}{T}\right)\right). \] Here \(\tau\) counts the steps since the start of the cycle. This gives a smooth transition from high to low learning rates. Many implementations first warm up the learning rate from a small value to \(\eta_0\), which we omit here.

In practice, the schedule restarts at \(\eta_0\) at the end of each cycle, and \(\tau\) restarts at 0. This cyclic pattern alternates exploration, with a high learning rate, and exploitation, with a low learning rate. Repeated cycles of heating and cooling similarly improve the structure of a metal. In non-convex problems it can help the model escape local minima while still allowing precise optimization. Figure 7.14(b) shows the cosine schedule with restarts, with the horizontal axis counting all training steps.

Regularization

As in Chapters 4 and 5, a model with many features can overfit. In the high-dimensional feature spaces that are common in astronomy, the model can easily fit noise in the training data instead of real structure. Regularization counters this problem by adding a penalty on large weights to the loss. When a line separates the classes perfectly, the loss keeps falling as the weights grow, and the penalty keeps the weights finite.

The standard approach, called L2 regularization or weight decay, adds a penalty proportional to the squared norm of the weight vector \[ E_{\text{reg}}(\mathbf{w}) = E(\mathbf{w}) + \lambda \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N [t_i \ln y_i + (1-t_i)\ln(1-y_i)] + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^D w_j^2. \] Here \(\lambda\) is the regularization strength, which we choose like the other hyperparameters, and \(D\) is the number of features. This modification changes the gradient that we use in the update, which becomes \[ \nabla E_{\text{reg}}(\mathbf{w}) = \nabla E(\mathbf{w}) + 2\lambda\mathbf{w} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - t_i) \mathbf{x}_i + 2\lambda\mathbf{w}. \]The new term \(2\lambda\mathbf{w}\) continuously pulls the weights toward zero during optimization, with a strength proportional to \(\lambda\). This keeps single weights from becoming very large. A very large weight would indicate that the model relies too much on one feature, a common sign of overfitting.

From a Bayesian perspective, this regularization corresponds to a Gaussian prior on the weights, as in linear regression (Chapter 5). The posterior distribution of the weights given the training data \(\mathcal{D}\) is proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})p(\mathbf{w}). \]Because \(E(\mathbf{w})\) is the loss per sample, the negative log-likelihood of the data is \(N E(\mathbf{w})\). We take a Gaussian prior on the weights with zero mean and variance \(1/(2N\lambda)\), so that the penalty scales with \(N\) like the likelihood \[ p(\mathbf{w}) \propto \exp\left(-N\lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\right). \] Maximizing the posterior is then equivalent to minimizing the negative log-posterior \[ -\ln p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}) = -\ln p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w}) - \ln p(\mathbf{w}) = N\left[E(\mathbf{w}) + \lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2\right] + \text{const}. \]

Regularization also balances bias and variance (Chapter 4). Bias is the systematic error that remains when the model is too rigid. Variance is how much the fitted model changes from one training set to another. Without regularization, the model might fit the training data closely but generalize poorly to new observations, a case of high variance. With very strong regularization, the model might not even fit the training data well, a case of high bias. The optimal \(\lambda\) balances the two, and in the Bayesian view it corresponds to the strength of our prior belief.

Regularization is particularly important for high-dimensional data such as spectra, where the number of features can exceed the number of training examples. When we classify stellar types from spectral features, regularization prevents the model from fitting noise at specific wavelengths. It favors broader patterns that hold across the spectrum.

7.9 Implementation Considerations

Even with well-chosen learning rates and batch sizes, an implementation needs safeguards against numerical problems that can corrupt the results.

Numerical Stability

The first problem arises in computing the cross-entropy loss, here averaged over a mini-batch of \(M\) samples \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^M [t_i \ln y_i + (1-t_i)\ln(1-y_i)]. \]The logarithm is problematic when a prediction \(y_i\) approaches 0 or 1. For \(y_i \approx 0\), \(\ln(y_i)\) tends to negative infinity, which causes numerical errors. A simple remedy is to add a small constant \(\epsilon\), typically \(10^{-7}\), so that the logarithm of zero cannot occur \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^M [t_i \ln(y_i + \epsilon) + (1-t_i)\ln(1-y_i + \epsilon)]. \]

We also need a numerically stable implementation of the sigmoid function itself \[ \sigma(z) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} & \text{if } z \geq 0 \\ \frac{e^z}{1 + e^z} & \text{if } z < 0 .\end{cases} \] This piecewise form avoids large exponentials that exceed the largest number the computer can store, an error called overflow. For large positive \(z\), computing \(e^{-z}\) is safer than computing \(e^z\), and the reverse holds for negative \(z\).

Optimization Pathologies

Training can encounter two pathologies. The first is vanishing gradients, where the length \(\|\nabla E(\mathbf{w})\|\) of the gradient becomes so small that the optimization stalls. The derivative of the sigmoid, \(\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\), approaches zero for large \(|z|\), because \(\sigma(z)\) approaches 0 or 1.

For logistic regression with the cross-entropy loss, however, this factor cancels in the gradient derived above. A wrong prediction with a probability close to 1 for the wrong class still gives the large gradient \((y_i - t_i)\mathbf{x}_i\). Vanishing gradients do arise with other losses, such as the squared error. Logistic regression keeps the sigmoid because its linear log-odds model requires it. Neural networks can use alternative activation functions, the nonlinear functions applied to the linear prediction, as we see in Chapter 15.

The second pathology is exploding gradients, where a “bad” batch containing outliers produces a huge step and can cause numerical overflow. For logistic regression, \(|y_i - t_i| \le 1\), so the gradient norm cannot exceed the norm of the largest feature vector, \(\|\nabla E\| \le \max_i \|\mathbf{x}_i\|\). Each step then moves the weights by at most \(\eta \max_i \|\mathbf{x}_i\|\). Explosions therefore arise mainly from features with very large values, which is one reason to standardize the features. Outliers are a common concern in astronomical applications, where they can arise from instrumental artifacts, cosmic rays or rare astrophysical phenomena.

We can detect a potential explosion by monitoring \(\max_j |w_j|\) during training. If the weights jump beyond reasonable bounds, say \(10^2\), we can apply gradient clipping, which scales down large gradients and keeps their direction \[ \nabla E_{\text{clipped}} = \min\left(1, \frac{\text{threshold}}{\|\nabla E\|}\right) \nabla E. \] Here \(\|\nabla E\|\) is the Euclidean norm of the full gradient vector and the threshold is a chosen constant. Clipping acts as a safety valve. It lets the optimization continue when outliers or other numerical instabilities, which are more common in complex models, temporarily make the gradients very large. Gradient clipping is common in the training of neural networks.

Monitoring and Early Stopping

Unlike linear regression, logistic regression has no closed-form solution, so we must decide when to stop the iterations. Rather than training for a fixed number of iterations, we evaluate the model on a validation set after each epoch. An epoch is a complete pass through the training data. When the validation error stops decreasing, we have likely reached the limit of what the data can teach. This “early stopping” strategy often works better than fixed iteration counts or gradient magnitude thresholds, and it provides a defense against overfitting.

Randomly shuffling the data between epochs keeps each batch representative of the overall distribution. This matters in astronomy, where objects may be ordered by position, brightness or observation time. Without shuffling, consecutive batches would each cover only one part of the sky or one range of brightness, so the gradient estimates would be biased.

Class Imbalance in Astronomy

Severe class imbalance is common in astronomical classification, especially in surveys where we search for rare objects among millions of background sources. For rare transient events such as supernovae, or for high-redshift quasars, the target class can be less than 0.1% of all objects. A model that predicts “not a transient” for each object would then reach at least 99.9% accuracy but fail at its primary task.

To address class imbalance, we can weight the minority class more heavily in the cross-entropy loss \[ E_{\text{weighted}}(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N [\omega_1 t_i \ln y_i + \omega_0 (1-t_i)\ln(1-y_i)], \] where \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_0\) are class weights. A common approach sets the weights inversely proportional to the class frequencies. If transients make up only 0.1% of the data set, for example, we might set \(\omega_1 = 0.999\) and \(\omega_0 = 0.001\). Each transient then counts 999 times more than each non-transient. This ensures that the rare class contributes meaningfully to the gradient despite its rarity.

This ends our study of binary classification. Chapter 8 extends logistic regression to more than two classes, such as stellar spectral types. It also revisits the cross-entropy loss through information theory and mutual information.

7.10 Tutorial: Classifying Red Clump Stars

This tutorial applies the logistic regression and gradient descent of this chapter to tell red clump stars from red giant branch stars. Red clump stars give precise distances across much of the Galaxy, but red giant branch stars look similar and spoil these distances. The full tutorial can be found at https://tingyuansen.github.io/statml/ as tutorial 7.

The two kinds of star are giants at different stages of stellar evolution. After a star exhausts the hydrogen in its core, it ascends the red giant branch, growing larger and more luminous. A larger star has a lower surface gravity, the strength of gravity at its surface. When the core ignites helium, the star becomes a red clump star. Red clump stars have nearly the same luminosity, so they are standard candles, sources of known luminosity whose apparent brightness gives their distance. Red giant branch stars span a wide range of luminosities, so one mistaken for a red clump star can have a less accurate distance.

To tell the two classes apart, astronomers use asteroseismology, the study of stellar oscillations, but it needs long monitoring and so covers small fields. Core helium burning makes the two classes differ in temperature and surface gravity, and spectroscopic surveys such as APOGEE measure both for far more stars. The tutorial trains a classifier on stars with known asteroseismic classes, so that it can classify stars outside those fields. In Section 4.8 the temperature was the output predicted from a spectrum. Here the temperature and gravity are two of eight features, and the output is a class (Section 7.1). The classes partly overlap in the temperature and gravity plane (Figure 7.15a), so a class probability tells more than a label alone.

Logistic regression gives these probabilities. It models the log-odds as linear in the features, and the sigmoid keeps the probability between 0 and 1 (Section 7.3). The weights are the unknowns, and stars with known classes set them.

We fit the weights to these stars by minimizing the cross-entropy loss that maximum likelihood defines. Unlike least squares, this loss barely penalizes stars far on the correct side of the boundary, so they do not dominate the fit (Section 7.6). Because the sigmoid is nonlinear, the loss has no closed-form minimum, so we descend it iteratively with gradient descent (Section 7.7). Small random batches of stars, as in stochastic gradient descent (Section 7.7.1), make each step computationally cheap for large samples.

The classifier is meant for stars outside those fields, so we check it on test stars that the fit does not use (Section 4.7). The check tests the linear decision boundary, a hyperplane that is a line in this plane, where the probability is one half. A line can fail when the classes have unequal covariances (Section 7.5), as their spread in gravity differs (Figure 7.15a). Here nearly all the test stars lie on the correct side of the line (Figure 7.15b), so a linear discriminant is enough.

A probability, unlike a label alone, lets a survey choose how many red giant branch stars it accepts. The survey keeps the stars above a chosen probability, and a higher threshold removes more red giant branch stars and some red clump stars too. The kept sample then has few red giant branch stars, so its distances can map the Galaxy. The same method applies to other classes in astronomy when a hyperplane in the feature space separates them well.

In the tutorial, a higher threshold raises the precision, the share of kept stars that are red clump stars. It lowers the recall, the share of red clump stars that we keep. The false positive rate is the share of red giant branch stars that we keep. The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the recall against the false positive rate for each threshold. It lies near the upper left corner for a good classifier. The area under it (AUC) does not depend on the threshold, so it can compare classifiers and the settings of one classifier.

A classifier turns a small labeled sample into labels for a whole survey. Asteroseismology classifies few stars, and spectroscopy measures far more, so a model trained on the first labels the second. Logistic regression suits this task, because its weights are easy to read and its probabilities say how far to trust each label. The red clump stars that it selects then map distances across the Galaxy, far beyond the reach of parallaxes.

Further Reading

Fisher (1936) developed linear discriminant analysis. Bliss (1934) introduced the probit model for binary responses, and Finney (1947) expanded it. Berkson (1944) applied the logistic function to the response of organisms to a dose, and Cox (1958) analyzed binary responses with several features. Shannon (1948) developed information theory, and Kullback and Leibler (1951) connected it to statistical inference through the KL divergence. Efron (1975) compared the efficiency of logistic regression and normal discriminant analysis. Rubinstein and Hastie (1997) and Ng and Jordan (2001) compared discriminative and generative learning. Cauchy (1847) described gradient descent, and Curry (1944) studied its convergence for nonlinear problems. Robbins and Monro (1951) developed the stochastic approximation behind stochastic gradient descent. Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) proposed a learning rate for stochastic gradient descent that falls along a cosine curve and restarts periodically. The tutorial follows the study of Ting et al. (2018), who selected red clump stars from spectra. Its asteroseismic classes come from the period spacings that Vrard et al. (2016) measured for Kepler red giants.
